text: Attack Surface Reduction rules in depth: what they actually block, the real rules worth knowing, and the audit-before-enforce rollout that keeps a new rule from breaking a legitimate business process on day one.

ASR rules, part of Microsoft Defender Exploit Guard, target specific behaviors malware relies on rather than scanning for known-bad files the way traditional antivirus signatures do. Ransomware and malicious macros rarely invent a new technique — they spawn a child process from Office, run an obfuscated script, or reach into lsass.exe for credentials, the same handful of moves over and over. Blocking the move itself, like this rule setting 'Block Office applications from creating child processes' to Audit mode, works against malware that didn't exist yet when the rule shipped.

Four real rules worth knowing by name: blocking Office from spawning a child process like cmd.exe or powershell.exe; blocking execution of obfuscated scripts trying to dodge detection; blocking Office macros from calling Win32 APIs directly, which lets a macro inject code without ever writing a file to disk; and blocking credential stealing from lsass.exe — the exact memory-access pattern Mimikatz-style credential dumping relies on, which ties directly into Lesson 15's Credential Guard and LSA Protection.

Each rule runs in one of four modes: Not configured, Block, Audit, or Warn. Audit mode logs Event ID 1125 every time the rule would have blocked something, without actually blocking it. Event ID 1121 is the same log entry once the rule is enforced in Block mode. That gap between the two IDs is exactly what makes a safe rollout possible.

A company runs the Office child-process rule in Audit mode fleet-wide for two weeks, then reviews the 1125 events through Microsoft Defender for Endpoint's ASR report. One legitimate hit turns up: a macro-driven Excel finance tool that spawns cmd.exe to kick off a nightly batch job. A targeted exclusion for that one workbook, a second audit pass to confirm it's clean, and only then does the rule flip to Block mode.

Enforced everywhere else, with no surprise outage on Finance's desk — that's the whole point of auditing before enforcing. Next up: Credential Guard and LSA Protection, stopping credential theft even after an attacker already has code running on the box.
